newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: UN SAYS NO TROOPS APPROVED FOR CONGO WITHOUT PEACE.
newsitem.headline: UN SAYS NO TROOPS APPROVED FOR CONGO WITHOUT PEACE.

text.p: The U.N. Security Council on Wednesday said that until fighting ended in the Congo Republic no peacekeeping force would be sent to Brazzaville.

In a statement read at a formal council meeting, the 15-member body called upon feuding factions "to halt all acts of violence immediately" and adhere to a July 13 cease-fire signed in Libreville under the leadership of Gabonese President Omar Bongo.

It said three conditions needed to be met before approval of a peacekeeping force -- a cease-fire, agreement for international control of the Brazzaville airport and a clear commitment for a negotiated military and political settlement.

"The Security Council is of the view that, despite some positive political developments, these conditions have not yet been fulfilled," said the statement read by the current council president, British Ambassador Sir John Weston.

Fighting broke out on June 5 after President Pascal Lissouba sent troops to surround the home of his predecessor, Denis Sassou Nguesso, as part of a crackdown on private militias. Hundreds of people died, many of them civilians killed by indiscriminate shelling, before the fragile cease-fire was signed in July

U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan and his special envoy for the region, Mohamed Sahnoun, have proposed an advance force of about 1,000 troops outside of the U.N. structure in an effort to organize it quickly. They want this force eventually to be increased and approved as a U.N. operation.
Some 17 African countries are ready to join such a force.
The entire venture has been tenuous from the start with reluctance among some countries, especially the United States, to sponsor another peacekeeping operation.

A peacekeeping force would be financed by all U.N. members whereby a multinational force would need voluntary funds from the participants or other interested countries. In either case, authorization from the 15-member Security Council is needed to give the operation legitimacy.

Sahnoun, who spoke to the council last month, warned that too many conditions set for a peace force might be self-defeating. "I noted that we could have a cease-fire for a week, we could have a cease-fire for 10 days, but we cannot guarantee a cease-fire forever because then we don't need a force." he said in July.
